The abstract discusses a study on Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in training deep neural networks. This method introduces constraints to the optimization process, improving the robustness of deep models. The constrained optimization problem is solved efficiently through semi-definite programming, and experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach in boosting adversarial robustness.

1544
The paper explores the convergence of deep neural networks when both weights and gradients are quantized to reduce storage and speed up inference. It finds that weight quantization introduces an error related to resolution and dimension, while gradient quantization slows convergence, which can be mitigated by clipping gradients before quantization. Empirical results support these findings, showing that quantized networks can train faster with performance comparable to full-precision models.

The extended Kalman filter (EKF) is a method for approximate Bayesian inference in non-conjugate models, linearizing the measurement function to avoid complex integrals. While it excels in real-time applications, its local nature is a limitation compared to global methods like variational inference or expectation propagation (EP). The paper introduces power EP, a nonlinear Kalman filter that improves EKF's linearization iteratively. This approach stabilizes EP and solves non-conjugate temporal Gaussian process models efficiently in linear time.

2019
GraphGAN is introduced as an implicit generative model for graphs, mimicking real-world networks by learning the distribution of biased random walks. It generates sibling graphs with similar properties using a stochastic neural network and the Wasserstein GAN objective. GraphGAN also maps latent inputs to graph properties, showing smooth transitions between different graph properties. It demonstrates strong generalization with good performance in link prediction and node classification.

By disentangling task inference and control, and using probabilistic filtering of latent task variables, the method allows agents to learn new tasks from limited experience. It outperforms existing algorithms significantly in both meta-training and adaptation efficiency across various benchmarks.

1270
### Summary:

The study introduces PolyGAN, a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that uses high-order polynomials as function approximators in the generator, represented by high-order tensors. The paper presents two tensor decompositions to reduce the number of parameters and implements them using hierarchical neural networks with linear/convolutional blocks. This approach allows a GAN generator to approximate data distributions without activation functions, achieving strong performance on both synthetic and real data, including images and 3D point clouds.

### Output:
The paper introduces Cross-View Training (CVT), a method for semi-supervised learning where a model acts as both teacher and student. The teacher produces soft targets for unlabeled data, which the student layers, each with limited input views, learn from. When combined with Virtual Adversarial Training, CVT enhances performance on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets. It also improves NLP tasks using large amounts of unlabeled data, outperforming supervised learning alone.

Graph Attention Networks (GATs) are introduced as a new type of neural network designed for graph-structured data. GATs have shown strong performance in both inductive and transductive tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, and protein-protein interaction datasets.

The paper addresses the adversarial-perturbation problem in neural networks, where small changes to input data can lead to incorrect classifications. The authors introduce a "goodness property" that confident regions of a good model should be well separated. The paper proposes embedding objectives and algorithms to improve the model's defense against adversarial attacks while maintaining good generalization.

Increasing the number of layers reduces the neuron requirement, which grows with the nth root of the number of variables, indicating that the optimal number of layers for practical use grows logarithmically with the number of variables.

2297
The study addresses the challenge of obtaining reliable uncertainty estimates from neural networks by introducing noise contrastive priors (NCPs). Unlike standard normal priors, NCPs train models to output high uncertainty for out-of-distribution data by adding noise to inputs and using a wide output distribution. This approach prevents overfitting and enhances the usefulness of uncertainty estimates for tasks like active learning. The method is demonstrated to be scalable and effective, particularly on the flight delays dataset.

The agent, leveraging the Go-Explore method, first identifies high-reward trajectories and then mimics them to solve the games. This approach outperforms existing methods, requires fewer interactions, and generalizes better to new games without action space restrictions.

The paper introduces a Synaptic Neural Network (SynaNN) inspired by neuroscience, featuring a nonlinear synapse model with excitatory and inhibitory channel probabilities. It defines a surprisal space and proves the topological conjugacy of inhibitory probability functions. The network includes a fully connected synapse graph and supports gradient descent and backpropagation for learning. A proof-of-concept experiment was conducted using an MNIST dataset with an MLP model incorporating the synapse network.

The study addresses why neural networks trained with Gradient Descent generalize well despite their ability to overfit. It proposes the "Coherent Gradients" hypothesis, suggesting that gradients from similar examples reinforce each other, leading to parameter changes that benefit many examples simultaneously. The hypothesis is supported by arguments and experiments, and it offers a modification to gradient descent to reduce overfitting.

The study explores the geometric properties of loss surfaces in deep learning, focusing on the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix. It compares the Empirical Hessian, calculated over an empirical dataset, and the True Hessian, derived from the data generating distribution. Using random matrix theory, the researchers show that the True Hessian has smaller eigenvalues. They validate this with experiments on ResNet and VGG-16 using different SGD schedules and introduce a fast spectral visualization framework.

The study examines why large, over-parameterized neural networks often generalize better than smaller ones, despite classical theory suggesting otherwise. Through extensive experiments with various models and datasets, the researchers find that well-generalizing networks are more robust to input perturbations near the training data. Factors like data augmentation and ReLU non-linearities improve this robustness, while poor practices like full-batch training or using random labels increase sensitivity. The input-output Jacobian norm is shown to predict generalization at the level of individual test points.

The paper addresses the instability in training generative adversarial networks (GANs) in high-dimensional spaces. DeepTD uses rank-1 tensor decomposition and is shown to be data-efficient, requiring only more samples than convolutional weights. Experiments support its effectiveness.

This paper addresses the challenge of reducing the memory footprint of deep neural networks to save energy, bandwidth, and storage. It introduces a method that encodes network weights using a random sample, controlling the compression rate by constraining the Kullback-Leibler divergence. This approach optimizes expected loss on the training set and achieves near-optimal performance on benchmark datasets like LeNet-5/MNIST and VGG-16/CIFAR-10.

The paper introduces "fidelity-weighted learning" (FWL), a semi-supervised student-teacher approach for training deep neural networks with both high-quality and weakly-labeled data. 381
The paper addresses the instability of training generative adversarial networks (GANs) in high-dimensional spaces, where the discriminator can easily classify most generated samples as fake. The proposed solution involves training a single generator against multiple discriminators, each focusing on different low-dimensional projections of the data. This approach ensures that the generator receives meaningful gradients throughout training, leading to higher-quality image samples compared to traditional single-discriminator training.

2290
The paper compares Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs), highlighting that VAEs use an explicit probability model for data generation while GANs do not. The study introduces an optimal transport GAN with entropy regularization, showing it can maximize a lower-bound on average sample likelihoods, similar to VAEs. This approach allows GANs to compute likelihood statistics, bridging the gap between the two methods. Numerical results support the theoretical findings.

The paper presents the Transductive Propagation Network (TPN), a new meta-learning framework designed to improve few-shot learning by classifying the entire test set at once. TPN addresses the low-data problem by propagating labels from labeled instances to unlabeled test instances using a learned graph construction module that leverages the data's manifold structure. It achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets by jointly learning feature embeddings and graph construction in an end-to-end manner.
